newsitem.title: USA: McGraw-Hill would consider exiting TV business.
newsitem.headline: McGraw-Hill would consider exiting TV business.

text.p: McGraw-Hill Cos. Inc. would consider exiting the television business if the right offer came along, President Harold McGraw III said.

While the company has no immediate plans to scale back its broadcasting operations, McGraw said in a recent interview the publishing giant would consider swapping the four TV stations it currently owns for a publishing or information business.

"I wouldn't be an aggressive acquirer of TV stations at this point," McGraw said on Thursday. "At the kind of premiums you'd have to pay, I don't think we can justify the returns we would want for our shareholders."
Asked if it planned to stay in broadcasting, McGraw said, "The answer to that is, right now, we're very happy with the broadcasting properties."

But he added that the company has "looked at many opportunities to potentially swap to some other areas that would be high-growth potential for us, consistent with other things we're doing. To date, (there's) nothing active, nothing pending."
He said the company would be open to an exchange for a "more pure information business," possibly to complement one of its publishing businesses.
McGraw said the company would consider an alliance or partnership as a way to more broadly distribute its various specialized data, including financial information.
"We've had several chats with people more directly tied to broadcasting operations," he said. "It could take on many forms."

In addition to its four ABC affiliate TV stations in Denver, San Diego, Indianapolis and Bakersfield, Calif., McGraw-Hill is the owner of the Standard & Poor's Corp. ratings service, Business Week magazine and other educational, professional and information products and services.
McGraw-Hill's stock edged down 31 cents to $61.875 on the New York Stock Exchange in early afternoon trading.
